source: Steele, Wen, Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
finding: First mechanistic test of Fauconnier. Models keep one low-rank 'space index' that tags which context (belief, painting, past, hypothetical) a value belongs to. One subspace trained on one space type also controls the others.
numbers: Transfer index 0.71-0.89 across Qwen2.5-3B, Pythia-2.8b, Falcon3-3B (Qwen 0.73 [0.67,0.78], Pythia 0.885, Falcon 0.711 [0.662,0.741]); bar of 0.7 fixed in advance; 160 held-out items per cell, 3 seeds.
quote: a subspace trained on one space type also controls the others, well above a random floor
limits: Open models of 3B scale mainly; shows a shared format in LMs, not the semantics of English. Falcon3 transfer is the lowest and borderline.
agent_relevance: Supports S2: a model can hold several scoped hypotheses at once with one tag mechanism, so explicit labelled spaces in the prompt fit how it already works.

source: Steele, Wen, Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
finding: Both the real value and the alternative value stay decodable after intervening text, so the model does not just store one colour token.
numbers: Qwen probe accuracy 0.96 [0.95,0.97] for base colour and 0.94 [0.94,0.95] for painting colour (chance 0.25, 3 seeds, 240 items per seed). Nine builders tested (painting, belief, dream, movie, past, yesterday, hypothetical, modal, reported speech): alternative-space accuracy 0.69-0.84, shuffled controls 0.25-0.27.
limits: Linear probes show decodability, not use. Varying surface frames weakens some base-space readouts (0.55-0.89).
agent_relevance: Scoped spaces survive across sentences, so listing hypotheses in separate labelled blocks is not fighting the model.

source: Steele, Wen, Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
finding: Binding is retrieval-shaped, not a persistent slot. Context bleeds: a distractor entity's colours decode at the target token almost as well as the target's own.
numbers: Target minus distractor decode advantage only +0.07 (Qwen) and +0.09 (Pythia); advantage falls to about 0 within about 16 filler sentences.
limits: Small models; the just-in-time profile matches other in-context representation work.
agent_relevance: Warning for S2: scoping is weak over long distance. Re-state the space label near the point of use; do not trust a label given 16+ sentences earlier.

source: Steele, Wen, Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
finding: Hand-built directions do not control the space; a learned low-rank subspace does. Rank 4 gives full control on Qwen.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B flip rate: random rank-1 0.583, diff-of-means rank-1 0.583, DAS rank-1 0.883, rank-2 0.967, rank-4/8/16 1.000. Three seeds: DAS rank-1 0.96 [0.88,1.00], diff-of-means 0.59, random 0.56 (200 items per seed). Pythia and Falcon3 reach 1.00 at rank 1.
limits: Single-model main table; 0.58 is a leakage floor, so only margins over it count.
agent_relevance: The space tag is compact and causal. Not directly usable by a prompt scaffold, but it argues the model does separate scopes internally.

source: Steele, Wen, Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
finding: Reporting a value and using it in a rule are causally separable. A subspace that flips the reported colour does not flip the rule conclusion, and the reverse.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B: colour-trained subspace flips colour 1.00, consequent 0.00; consequent-trained flips consequent 1.00, colour 0.32. Principal-angle cosine 0.11 (Qwen), 0.17 (Falcon3). Falcon3 less clean; Pythia uninterpretable (baseline near chance).
limits: Only one model gives the clean double dissociation.
agent_relevance: Fits the faithfulness gap: what a model says in a space may not be the value it reasons with. S8 should check conclusions, not only stated values.

source: Steele, Wen, Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
finding: Space-builders compose: nesting (a painting inside a belief) mints a new router over the shared slot. Time spaces transfer too.
numbers: Future-space flip 0.81, 0.90, 0.83 across three families (single seed). Past-present transfer 0.90 with random floor 0.03 (present to past 1.00, past to present 0.91). Nested readouts needed clean-accuracy gates of 0.80.
limits: Nested results depend on gating by clean accuracy; slot-reuse magnitude is Qwen2.5-14B only.
agent_relevance: Nested hypotheses (a belief about a hypothesis) are handled by the model but need gates; test nesting depth in our own evals.

source: Steele, Wen, Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
finding: Belief is not specially separated from other space types, against the formal-semantics view. The subspace recovers only a coarse taxonomy.
numbers: Belief modal/hypothetical transfer above the ordinary between-class baseline by +0.08 (Qwen), +0.03 (Pythia), +0.09 (Falcon3). Qwen2.5-14B readout transfer: belief 0.74/0.79, counterfactual 0.33/0.86, depictive 0.64/0.51 (asymmetric).
limits: Difference between class and within class is only +0.16 to +0.37; a hyperintensional boundary would be hard to detect.
agent_relevance: Treat belief, counterfactual and hypothetical scopes with the same machinery; no special belief handling needed in S2.

source: Steele, Wen, Han (2026) One mechanism for many mental spaces: a shared router over a value slot in language models
finding: Behaviour at frontier scale: stating bindings is easy, deriving values by rule under load is the hard part. Space binding shows no capacity curve from 1 to 4 spaces.
numbers: gpt-4o, Qwen-72B, Gemini-2.5, GPT-4.1, Claude, Llama-70B: 1.00 stated binding up to K=8 objects (16 queried cells), swap 0.00. Derived K8 inference 1.00 for strong models; Llama-8B 0.31, another set 0.90. Open 3B models flat across 1-4 spaces (Qwen 0.95/0.93/0.85/0.91 for K1-K4).
limits: Frontier numbers are behavioural only; API gives no activations. Pythia at chance floor.
agent_relevance: S2 can keep many spaces safely if they are stated. Risk is in derived values, so S4 should test derived consequences inside each space.

source: Steele et al. (2026) companion paper on belief in mental spaces (cited by the main paper; not located)
finding: Cited as separating a 'value slot' from a 'router': at the value token a subspace transfers across frames (belief to reality 89-95% of own effect); at the query position the routers are near-orthogonal.
numbers: Cross-frame transfer at query position below 0.3 of own-frame effect; Qwen, Mistral, OLMo-2.
limits: Second-hand figures taken from the main paper; companion text not found and not opened.
agent_relevance: Value storage is shared, selection is by query. The prompt should name the space in the question itself.

source: Wilf et al. (2023) Think Twice: Perspective-Taking Improves Large Language Models' Theory-of-Mind Capabilities (SimToM)
finding: A two-step prompt (first keep only what character X knows, then answer) acts as a hand-made scoped space. It beats single prompts and CoT on false-belief items.
numbers: ToMI false-belief: GPT-4 0-shot 25.5, CoT 74.25, SimToM 87.75; GPT-3.5 67.25 / 34.0 / 81.0. BigToM false-belief: GPT-3.5 41.0 / 56.25 / 70.5; Llama2-7b 47.5 / 31.5 / 70.5. 200 BigToM and 1000 ToMI questions, temperature 0.
quote: LLMs are substantially stronger at ToM reasoning than they appear when probed with a single inference pass.
limits: GPT-4 on BigToM false belief: SimToM 92.0 vs CoT 93.25 (no gain; GPT-4 made the data). Llama2-7b true-belief falls 65.75 to 44.0.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S2/S1 scoping: filter context to one scope, then reason inside it. Gains are largest for weaker models.

source: Wilf et al. (2023) Think Twice: Perspective-Taking Improves Large Language Models' Theory-of-Mind Capabilities (SimToM)
finding: Ablation: both steps must be separate. Merging into one prompt, or replacing perspective with generic reasoning, loses most of the gain.
numbers: GPT-3.5 ToMI false-belief: SimToM 81.0, SimToM-Single 58.75, SimToM-Multi (reasoning step) 31.75. BigToM FB: 70.5 / 50.75 / 37.25. Few-shot domain examples 85.5 (ToMI), 90.5 (BigToM). Oracle human perspective 96 / 96.
limits: Self-consistency 33.5 on ToMI FB and Tree-of-Thoughts also below SimToM. Perspective was made only by hiding events, not inferring.
agent_relevance: Keep the scoping call separate from the reasoning call. Oracle 96 shows scope quality is the bottleneck.

source: Wilf et al. (2023) Think Twice: Perspective-Taking Improves Large Language Models' Theory-of-Mind Capabilities (SimToM)
finding: Single-pass models often answer about the world state instead of the character's belief; GPT-4 zero-shot first-order true-belief on ToMI was near floor.
numbers: GPT-4 ToMI FO-T 2.0 (0-shot), 63.0 (CoT), 95.0 (SimToM); SO-T 49.0 / 85.5 / 80.5. Llama refusals pull scores below chance.
limits: The odd GPT-4 0-shot ToMI collapse suggests prompt-format sensitivity; only English, instruction-tuned models, none under 7B.
agent_relevance: Failure mode to guard: answering in the wrong space. S8 can ask 'which space does this answer belong to?'.

source: Sclar et al. (2023) Minding Language Models' (Lack of) Theory of Mind: A Plug-and-Play Multi-Character Belief Tracker (SymbolicToM)
finding: Explicit system outside the model: code builds nested belief graphs per character (a global graph plus nested graphs B_p1..pk, depth 2), then the LM answers a simplified question from the right graph. This is a mental-space machine built by code.
numbers: ToMi: GPT-3 davinci +38 points to 92% average; Flan-T5-XL +62 on first-order false belief; GPT-3.5 +78 on second-order. D1/D2/D3 (100 stories each): LLaMA-7B 99/92/88 (gains +82/+75/+71); GPT-3.5 third-order 8% to 100%. Finetuned GPT-3 gets 51/68/32; TTT 49/65/78.
quote: dramatically enhances off-the-shelf neural networks' theory of mind in a zero-shot setting
limits: Needs chronological stories; NLI and OpenIE errors propagate; witness rule assumes all in a location see all; Sally-Anne family only. Flan-T5-XL drops 10 on D1 (86 to 76). Memory grows exponentially with depth.
agent_relevance: Shows code-held scoped state beats model-held state, and generalises out of domain where finetuning does not. Argues for S2 spaces kept by code in the scaffold.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM: A Benchmark for Stress-testing Machine Theory of Mind in Interactions
finding: Information-asymmetric conversations with several question types per fact. Models answer single questions but fail when consistency across question types is required.
numbers: 13 models. Humans All* 87.5. Best model GPT-4 0613 + CoT: All* 18.4, All 26.6 (without CoT All* 8.2, All 12.3); BeliefQ[Choice] 80.6 (73.3 without CoT); AnswerabilityQ 40.2; InfoAccessQ 57.7. Fine-tuned Flan-T5-XL All* 26.5 (zero-shot 0.0) but still weak on consistency.
quote: illusory or false sense of ToM capabilities
limits: Small human baseline (11 students, 32 sets); LLM-generated small talk; 8.6% of sets removed. Text only.
agent_relevance: Test scoped state with several probing questions per fact; one correct answer can hide a broken scope.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM: A Benchmark for Stress-testing Machine Theory of Mind in Interactions
finding: CoT trades one error for another: fewer inclusion errors but more exclusion errors for most models. Full conversations are worse than short ones.
numbers: GPT-4 0613 All* 8.2 to 18.4 with CoT. For list questions models mainly include characters who are unaware. Several binary scores at or below the 50 baseline.
limits: Effect of CoT varies by model; for some, All-for-each-character fell.
agent_relevance: CoT alone does not fix scoping. A per-character scoped list built before answering (as in SimToM) targets the dominant error.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Hi-ToM: A Benchmark for Evaluating Higher-Order Theory of Mind Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Nested beliefs (she thinks he thinks...) break models as order rises. Accuracy falls from near perfect at order 0 to near zero at order 4.
numbers: Overall: GPT-4 (32k) 60.42 standard, 64.04 with CoT prompt; Claude-instant 49.33/52.33; GPT-3.5-turbo 28.67/35.67; Guanaco-65B 33.33/35.00 (table column layout hard to parse). GPT-4 above 20% at order 4. Deceptive messages (0 to 4) lower GPT-4 joint accuracy by 32%, 18.1%, 16%, 11% across orders. CoT gain about 7 (GPT-3.5), 3.6 (GPT-4).
quote: All the LLMs we evaluate exhibit less than 60% accuracy scores
limits: Only four models; RLHF effect not studied; scripted dialogue. Position bias: better when the answer is the first or last container.
agent_relevance: Nesting depth is a hard limit for in-head spaces. Beyond order 2, write each nested space as its own block.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Hi-ToM: A Benchmark for Evaluating Higher-Order Theory of Mind Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Manual review of 300 wrong answers gave five causes, the first being too little reasoning depth.
numbers: Causes: skipping steps and answering a lower order, commonsense error, hallucination, temporal confusion, spurious causal inference.
limits: Based on 300 responses.
agent_relevance: Make S2 force one explicit line per nesting level so depth cannot be skipped.

source: Gandhi et al. (2023) Understanding Social Reasoning in Language Models with Language Models (BigToM)
finding: Causal-template benchmark of 5,000 items. Models are fine on forward belief but fail backward belief, which needs inferring the agent's earlier percept.
numbers: GPT-4 0-shot, TB and FB together: forward belief .97 (.90 with initial belief), forward action .79 (.90), backward belief .40 (.40). Others, forward belief: llama-65b .51/.41, davinci-003 .65/.25, gpt-3.5 .53/.31, claude-1.3 .81/.59, claude-2 .68/.52. Humans about 82% (TB) and 72% (FB) on backward belief; 20 participants.
limits: GPT-4 wrote the items (checked with a Claude-2 set; GPT-4 scored similarly); 2-3% of templates malformed. Two-option questions.
agent_relevance: Stating an initial belief makes most models anchor on it and score worse: a stated view inside a space leaks into the answer. Supports putting suspect material in a marked block (S1 input hygiene).

source: Gandhi et al. (2023) Understanding Social Reasoning in Language Models with Language Models (BigToM)
finding: One-shot prompting helps consistently; zero-shot CoT does not. One-shot CoT helps but may be template copying.
numbers: Prompts: 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, 1-shot, 1-shot CoT, temperature 0.
limits: Gain from CoT may reflect copying, not ToM.
agent_relevance: Examples inside the scaffold matter more than 'think step by step'.

source: Ullman (2023) Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the logic of a false-belief task reverse a claimed success. Argues failures count more than averages.
numbers: No numbers read: only the abstract was opened.
quote: outlying failure cases should count for more than average success rates
limits: Abstract only; later models likely handle many alterations, see SimToM and BigToM.
agent_relevance: Test scopes with altered variants, not only canonical items.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of Language Models Through Counterfactual Tasks
finding: Counterfactual worlds (base-9 addition, swapped chess pieces, flipped spatial axes) make accuracy fall sharply. Models partly recite default-world procedures.
numbers: 11 tasks; GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude-v1.3, PaLM-2. Some arithmetic accuracy falls from near perfect to near zero; bases 8 and 16 easier than 9 and 11. Up to 16 few-shot examples narrow the gap but leave a large one for bases 9, 11, 16. Appendix C table not read.
quote: performance substantially and consistently degrades compared to the default conditions
limits: Counterfactual tasks may simply be harder; shortcuts in FOLIO; open models excluded. Zero-shot CoT sometimes hurt (PaLM-2 base-10 and 16 addition; GPT-4 chord task).
agent_relevance: A counterfactual space must override the default world; the model leaks default rules into it. Run a counterfactual comprehension check before reasoning inside it.

source: Feng and Steinhardt (2024) How do Language Models Bind Entities in Context?
finding: Models attach abstract binding IDs to entities and attributes; these are additive vectors in a continuous subspace.
numbers: Swapping IDs: control accuracy about 99%, one swap under 3%, double swap restores over 97%. Transfer across tasks 0.71-0.88 vs about 0.30 for zero or random vectors. Pythia and LLaMA families, sharper with scale.
limits: Not universal: multiple-choice uses direct binding; attribute interventions fail on multi-token bios.
agent_relevance: This is the entity-binding mechanism the mental-space router sits on; scoping into spaces reuses it.

source: Kim and Schuster (2023) Entity Tracking in Language Models
finding: Tracking changing state (7 boxes, up to 12 operations) works only in models with code in pretraining or finetuning, and degrades with more operations.
numbers: 2,200 scenarios, 91 test examples each. text-davinci-003 the only model consistently above a strong random baseline; all contents right in over 25% of cases after 7 operations. Flan-T5 and GPT-3 davinci mostly repeat the initial state. GPT-4 well above GPT-3.5. Finetuned T5-base near perfect; trained on at most 2 operations it still exceeds 45% on longer ones. Reanalysis: an always-initial-state baseline scores 62.7% on Li et al. Alchemy.
quote: pretraining on text corpora alone does not make this capacity surface
limits: Behavioural only; may need more working memory than humans have; English only.
agent_relevance: Long state updates inside one space are unreliable; restate state each step rather than trusting silent tracking.

source: Li, Nye, Andreas (2021) Implicit Representations of Meaning in Neural Language Models
finding: Linear probes read entity state from BART and T5 hidden states; swapping encoded states changes generation.
numbers: Full-state recovery 14.3% of Alchemy and 53.8% of TextWorld examples (T5); state sits at the entity's last mention in TextWorld.
limits: Simple synthetic domains; probe may miss nonlinear encoding; later reanalysis shows the Alchemy baseline is strong.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that situation models exist inside LMs, tied to mentions of the entity; state labels near the entity help.

source: Prakash et al. (2025) Language Models Use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
finding: Belief tracking uses three lookbacks: bind character and object ordering IDs to state, retrieve the answer, and a visibility lookback that updates an observer's beliefs.
numbers: Llama-3-70B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-405B, Qwen2.5-14B; CausalToM stories; interchange interventions on 80 correct cases per model; layers roughly: binding 20-38, answer 34-56, visibility 10-31. No behavioural accuracies seen in the text read.
limits: Two-character stories, three models; visibility payload semantics unconfirmed; appendix D cut off.
agent_relevance: Belief scopes are looked up by pointer, so each scope needs a stable label. Explicit 'who saw what' lines help the visibility step.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: Agent-loop use of separate hypotheses: generate several abstract rules, make each a program, test on examples. Each hypothesis is its own scoped candidate.
numbers: 100-problem ARC subset: direct prompting 17%, LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected hypotheses 33%.
limits: Abstract only opened; other benchmarks not read.
agent_relevance: Same shape as S2 plus S4: separate candidate rules, each tested alone. Close to our ARC control.
